headline: Whitney: gas stations hold 15% of hemp licences, 2.6% of revenue
dek: Economist Beau Whitney told a Washington summit on 18 November that oversupply, not hemp, is squeezing licensed cannabis: 123M lb of capacity, 15-20M lb sold.
key_points: Whitney Economics says gas stations hold about 15% of US hemp retail licences but generate 2.6% of hemp revenue.
Beau Whitney put licensed US cannabis production capacity at about 123 million pounds against 15 million to 20 million pounds of legal sales.
He said hemp competes directly with licensed cannabis in edibles and leads in beverages, while licensed cannabis dominates flower and pre-rolls.
The firm's 2026 report, based on 496 self-reported survey responses, values the hemp cannabinoid market at $30.2 billion to $38.7 billion.
body: Two claims run through the fight in Washington over hemp-derived THC. One is that the trade is a gas-station business. The other is that it is the reason licensed cannabis companies are losing money. An economist who has studied both markets told a policy summit this week that his data support neither.

Beau Whitney, founder of Whitney Economics, presented the findings on Wednesday 18 November at the IgniteIt Cannabis Capital & Policy Summit in Washington, D.C., according to IgniteIt's own report of the session. Gas stations, he said, hold about 15% of hemp retail licences nationwide and generate 2.6% of hemp revenue. And licensed cannabis, he argued, has a bigger problem than hemp: it can grow many times more than it can legally sell.
## The gas station numbers

The 15% and 2.6% figures come from Whitney's national survey of hemp businesses combined with public licensing records. The gap between them means the average gas station sells far less hemp product than the average specialist: on these numbers, a gas station licence brings in roughly a sixth of the revenue of a typical hemp retail licence.

That does not settle the policy argument. IgniteIt's report notes that the data say nothing about product safety, age checks or oversight at those outlets. A channel can be small in revenue and still be where most of the problems are. But it does change the picture of where the money is. Most hemp cannabinoid revenue, on this evidence, runs through dedicated hemp shops, smoke and vape stores and other channels, not through forecourts.

The firm's written report explains why licence counts mislead. Several states, including Florida, Texas, Georgia and North Carolina, issue hemp retail permits to convenience stores in large numbers, which inflates the count of retailers without adding much in sales. Whitney Economics says it adjusted its retailer estimates downward in those states for that reason.
## Where hemp and cannabis actually compete

Whitney's second argument is that the overlap between the two markets is narrower than the debate assumes. Licensed cannabis still dominates flower and pre-rolls, he said. Hemp-derived products are stronger in beverages, which remain a small category inside licensed cannabis. Edibles are the real contested ground, and he acknowledged that hemp products are taking business there.

For a licensed operator, that maps onto the product mix. A company that lives on flower is competing mostly with other licensed growers and with the illicit market. A company built on gummies and drinks is competing with hemp.
## The oversupply case

The figure that matters most to cannabis investors is the capacity gap. Whitney put licensed US production capacity at about 123 million pounds a year, against an estimated 15 million to 20 million pounds of legal sales. On his numbers, the industry is licensed to produce between six and eight times what the legal market buys.

He argued that this, more than hemp, explains falling wholesale prices and thin margins. He also explained why the glut does not clear. A grain farmer facing low prices can plant something else. A licensed cannabis grower mostly cannot. Federal restrictions, debt and limited access to bankruptcy protection leave many operators with little choice but to keep producing, even below cost.
> If growers are licensed for six to eight times what the market buys, a hemp ban moves the price of an edible, not the price of a pound.

The implication, as IgniteIt's report puts it, is that restricting hemp to protect licensed cannabis would do little for the industry's underlying finances. That is Whitney's conclusion from his own data, and it is a contested one: licensed operators in several states say hemp beverages and edibles are taking their customers. Both things can be true at once.
## What the full report says
The presentation builds on the Whitney Economics 2026 U.S. Hemp Cannabinoid Report. We read the report. Its headline numbers:

The hemp-derived cannabinoid market is put at $30.2 billion to $38.7 billion a year, with the upper figure described as up 36% since the firm's 2023 study. The sector employs 351,855 workers at the midpoint, earning $13.9 billion in wages. The supply chain adds $18.8 billion in business revenue, not counting cultivation. The firm counts between 44,000 and 76,000 hemp-related businesses. States could collect $1.7 billion to $2.1 billion in sales tax on these products.

On the federal ban, the survey's respondents said that if the 2025 legislation stays in place, more than 70% of businesses would close or move abroad. The report translates that into 225,861 jobs and $8.9 billion in wages lost. At the summit, Whitney also gave a wider figure of $175 billion for the total addressable US hemp market across fibre, grain and industrial uses, with cannabinoids about 22% of it.
## How much weight to put on it

Three cautions, all ours. First, the survey is self-reported. It drew 496 responses from 35 states in June and July 2026, and business owners asked about a law that threatens them have every reason to answer forcefully. The closure estimate is a statement of intent, not a forecast tested against what firms actually did.

Second, the report says Whitney Economics was asked to refresh its 2023 study, and the copy in circulation is hosted on a hemp industry campaign website. The research was done for a side in the debate. That does not make the licence and revenue data wrong, but readers should know where it comes from.

Third, the capacity figure measures what licences allow, not what was grown. Licensed canopy that sits idle does not depress prices. The gap is still large enough that the direction of the argument holds.
## What to watch

Watch 11 December, when the federal ban on most hemp-derived THC products is due to take effect. Watch the Hemp Guardrails Act from Senators Tim Sheehy and Amy Klobuchar, which we covered on 18 November, and whether any hemp language is attached to a year-end spending bill. Watch whether licensed operators or their trade groups publish data that answers Whitney's capacity figure. And watch state licence counts: if regulators begin reporting hemp revenue by type of outlet, the gas-station question can be settled with tax records instead of surveys.
